1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: The natural recapture: the knight takes the centre and the bishops and queen get open lines. It will be harassed by Black's developing moves, so White's piece set-up must be ready to meet them, but the central knight also supports a later attack.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.c3.name: Sicilian Defence: Smith-Morra Gambit Deferred
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.c3.strategy: A gambit that offers a pawn for a lead in development and an open c-file. Black keeps a real extra pawn that White must justify by quick development, so the idea only works if White's pieces come out faster than Black can untangle.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which stands in the centre but can be hit at once: ...Nc6 attacks it with a gain of time and the queen has to go back. White's structure stays healthy, so the damage is a tempo, but it gives Black the easier development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6.name: Sicilian Defence: Kan Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6.strategy: A flexible waiting move: it rules out Nb5 and prepares ...b5, and Black delays developing the knights until White commits. The cost is a tempo that does not develop a piece; Black bets on a compact structure and counterplay on the queenside.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6.name: Sicilian Defence: Taimanov Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on the d4-knight and keeps all of Black's options open for the bishops and the queen. White can challenge or exchange the knight, but Black gets natural development in a flexible position.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.name: Sicilian Defence: French Variation, Normal
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4 and stops the quick e5 push, since ...Qa5+ would then win the pawn. Black keeps a flexible set-up and makes White defend the e-pawn before anything else.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Qb6.name: Sicilian Defence: Kveinis Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Qb6.background: A pet line of the Lithuanian International Master Aloyzas Kveinys (1962–2018), it has also been played by strong grandmasters including Nigel Short and Judit Polgar.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Qb6.strategy: A sharp surprise weapon: the queen hits the d4-knight and the b2-pawn at once and prepares to bring the bishop to bear on f2. A calm retreat of the knight to b3 takes the sting out, and Black has committed the queen early.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5.name: Sicilian Defence: Paulsen-Basman Defence
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5.strategy: Develops with an attack on the d4-knight, but the knight can retreat with a gain of time. It is an offbeat way to develop that leaves Black chasing the initiative, though the position stays playable.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.B.name: Sicilian Defence: Kan Variation, Modern Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.B.strategy: The most popular reply: the bishop develops, guards e4 and commits no pawns. White keeps a flexible, harmonious set-up and can still choose between a central plan and a kingside attack.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.c.name: Sicilian Defence: Kan Variation, Maróczy Bind, Réti Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.c.strategy: Clamps down on d5 and gains space with pawns on c4 and e4, so Black's freeing ...d5 break is held back. White accepts slower development for a lasting space advantage; Black has to find counterplay against the bind.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.N.name: Sicilian Defence: Kan Variation, Knight Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.N.strategy: Develops and guards e4, and it makes an early ...Nf6 awkward, since e5 would then hit the knight and fix a weakness on d6. Black first has to control e5, so White gets a head start in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.B.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4, which the bishop already guards, so the pawn is tied to White's pieces. Black keeps a solid, flexible set-up with pawns on a6 and e6 and decides the rest of the plan after White commits.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.B.name: Sicilian Defence: Kan Variation, Polugaevsky Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.B.strategy: Develops with an attack on the d4-knight, but the knight can retreat with a gain of time. The bishop then has to find a safe square, and the natural retreat can leave Black's kingside awkward, so Black must know the line.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.B.name: Sicilian Defence: Kan Variation, Swiss Cheese Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.B.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto of the king's bishop, but Black delays the development of the other pieces and loosens the kingside structure. White simply develops and builds on a lead in the centre.
Castles before committing the centre: the king is safe and e4 stays solidly guarded by the bishop on d3. White keeps the choice between central and kingside plans open.

Brings the last minor piece into play and guards e4 with a piece, so the centre is solid and the king can castle with everything in place. The knight can be pinned by a bishop on b4, but e4 stays defended, so the pin does no harm.

Defends e4 and prepares to castle, and keeps the queen's knight free to choose its square. Black meets it with ordinary development, so White gets a flexible but modest set-up with a small space edge.
Solid: the pawn takes control of e5, so White's e-pawn cannot advance for free. Black heads for a compact set-up and castling, and has to know how to meet an attack on the kingside.

Guards e5 from the side, so White's e-pawn cannot advance for free, and keeps the d-pawn flexible. The queen also eyes h2 along the diagonal and the c-file, giving Black counterplay against White's kingside plans.
Attacks the d4-knight at once, but the knight steps back with a threat on the bishop, so Black loses a tempo retreating it. In return the bishop keeps an active diagonal towards f2.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.c.strategy: Develops and attacks e4, which nothing defends yet, so White must spend a move on it. Black uses the tempo to bring out the king's knight, though the bind on d5 means Black still has to fight for freedom.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.c.name: Sicilian Defence: Kan Variation, Maróczy Bind, Hedgehog Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.c.strategy: Meets the clamp with a fianchetto: the bishop on g7 will bear down on the d4-knight along the long diagonal. The plan costs time while White's pawns on c4 and e4 take space, so Black's position stays cramped.
Checks at once to make White decide how to meet the bishop. A knight block leads into the familiar pin set-up; a bishop trade eases Black's cramp, since the side with less space gains from exchanges.
Defends e4 while developing, and keeps the bind: with c4 and e4 both supported, White holds the d5 square and a space edge.

Defends e4 and heads for castling, a straightforward set-up that keeps the clamp of c4 and e4. The bishop blocks the queen's protection of the d4-knight, so Black can attack it, though the knight can step away with tempo.
Defends both e4 and the d4-knight with the queen and keeps the clamp of c4 and e4 intact. The cost is that the queen blocks the f1-bishop's diagonal, so development and castling take longer.

Pins the knight against the king, so it can no longer guard e4 and Black threatens to take the pawn. White has to defend e4 at once, while Black gets a comfortable game without weakening the pawn structure.

Places the queen where it covers e5 and presses on the c-file, in front of the c4-pawn that clamps Black's centre. Black keeps every set-up open; the price is that the queen can be hit by a developing move such as a bishop on f4.

Builds a solid pawn set-up: the d-pawn holds e5, the pawns on a6, d6 and e6 form a compact block, and Black waits for a chance to free the game with a central break. The price is space, since White's pawns on c4 and e4 keep Black passive.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.N.name: Sicilian Defence: Kan Variation, Wing Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.N.strategy: Starts the queenside attack at once, aiming to drive away the knight that guards e4 and to bring the bishop to the long diagonal against the pawn. It spends time and loosens the queenside, so White can strike back in the centre.

The main Kan move: the queen covers e5, so ...Nf6 can follow without White's e5 driving the knight back, and it already presses the c3 knight along the open file. Black keeps a flexible set-up and develops only once White has shown its plan.

Develops with a challenge to the d4 knight, and ...a6 has already stopped Nb5. The cost is the trade on c6: after Nxc6 bxc6 White develops naturally against the damaged queenside pawns, and Black has to work to reach equality.

Controls e5 with a pawn, so ...Nf6 can follow, and builds the compact pawn pair on d6 and e6. A solid, flexible choice, but it commits the d-pawn early and lets White choose freely between quiet development and a pawn storm on the kingside.

Supports e4 and eyes the b5-pawn, so the long-diagonal pressure Black planned meets a solid defence. White develops naturally and keeps the centre intact while Black's queenside advance has loosened Black's own camp.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.N.name: Sicilian Defence: Kan Variation, Wing Attack, Fianchetto Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 a6 5.N.strategy: Meets the pressure on e4 with a fianchetto: the bishop on g2 guards the pawn and contests the diagonal. It is a sound but slower and less natural way to defend than the bishop on d3, and does nothing against Black's queenside advance.

Develops the bishop to a safe square and keeps the queen's guard on the d4 knight. It does less for e4, though: ...b4 chases the c3 knight off its post and Black's bishop then hits an unguarded pawn, so White has to react to Black's plan.

Attacks the d4 knight, which nothing defends because Bd3 blocks the queen's guard, so White has to spend a tempo on it. Black keeps the queenside storm in reserve (...b4 to chase the c3 knight, ...Bb7 against e4) and gains time for it.

Puts the bishop on the long diagonal against e4, which the knight and the bishop both guard, so nothing is threatened yet. Black keeps the queen at home, prepares ...b4 to chase the knight and keeps ...Qb6 in reserve against the loose d4 knight.

Challenges the d4 knight, which Bd3 has left without the queen's support, so White must trade or retreat. After Nxc6 dxc6 Black has a sound pawn chain and an open d-file, but the position is passive and the queenside advance has lost its point.

Puts the bishop on the long diagonal against e4, which only the c3 knight guards: the point of the whole ...b5 advance. With ...b4 ready to chase that knight, White has to shore up e4 with the fianchettoed bishop and accept a slower, more strategic fight.

Develops with a challenge to the d4 knight. Recapturing on c6 with the d-pawn gives Black a sound pawn chain and an open d-file, but the move forgets the long diagonal against e4 that the advance ...b5 was played for, so White finishes the fianchetto in peace.

Chases the c3 knight at once: on a4 it is offside and no longer guards e4, which ...Bb7 can then attack. White answers by finishing the fianchetto, so Black gains a little time but loosens the queenside for it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Taimanov Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..background: It is more common nowadays than 5.Nb5.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..strategy: The main move: it develops a piece, defends e4 and keeps the strong knight on d4. White's development is harmonious and leaves Black to find a plan against the central knight, while White chooses between a quiet game and a kingside attack.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Taimanov Variation, Szén Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..strategy: Jumps at the d6 hole that ...e6 left behind: with the queen on the open d-file it threatens Nd6+, which would win the bishop pair. White commits the knight to an outpost it cannot keep and loses time later, so this sharp sideline is a test more than a main line.

Gains space: the c4 pawn takes d5 away and clamps the centre. But without a pawn on d6 Black is not cramped yet: Black can hit e4 and pin the knight that comes to c3, and reaches comfortable equality. A space-grabbing try that gives White little.

The main way to meet the threat on d6: 5...a6? allows Nd6+ and the bishop pair. The pawn closes the hole and prepares ...a6 to chase the b5 knight, which then needs several moves to get back into play.

Answers the threat on d6 by hitting the unprotected e4 pawn: after Nd6+ Bxd6 Qxd6, ...Nxe4 attacks the queen and wins a pawn, so White normally defends e4 first. Black can still choose a solid pawn on d6 or a pin on the c3 knight, but the d6 hole remains a worry.

Attacks the knight but ignores the threat: Nd6+ Bxd6 Qxd6 gives White the bishop pair and a queen on d6 that cramps Black's whole position. Black is behind in development and has nothing to show for it.

Grabs space: the c4 pawn defends the b5 knight and takes d5 away, so Black cannot free the game with ...d5 and has to play a slow, cramped but solid game. The price is time, since the knight will be chased, and a weakened d4 square.

Invites ...e5, which weakens d5 and gives White a hole to aim at once the bishop has dropped back to e3. The idea is sound but slow: the bishop moves twice, and the knight on b5 is still waiting to be chased by ...a6.

Develops the second knight and guards e4, a natural way to bring the pieces out. But it leaves the knight on b5 to be chased away by ...a6, and without the c4 clamp on d5 White has no particular advantage while the moves spent on one knight are a real cost.

Attacks the undefended e4 pawn, so White has to commit another piece to its defence, while Black prepares ...a6 to kick the b5 knight. White ends up moving the same knight again and again for space; Black trades time for a compact, solid set-up and counterplay against the pawn centre.

Chases the knight at once, but it simply returns to c3, where it guards e4 and keeps the c4 pawn's grip on d5. Black gets a pawn move that is useful anyway, yet the knight is not driven to a poor square.

A safe developing move that prepares castling and keeps the bishop behind the d6 pawn. It leaves the b5 knight unchallenged for the moment and puts no pressure on e4, so White gets time to arrange its pieces around the c4 clamp.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Taimanov Variation, Bastrikov Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..strategy: The most usual move: the queen covers d6 and e5, eyes the c-file and leaves Black free to organise queenside play with pawn moves and the c8 bishop. White cannot gain time with e5, but the queen can become a target for a knight.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Four Knights Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..strategy: Develops with an attack on e4 and prepares ...Bb4 to pin the c3 knight. Black gets quick development, but the f6 knight can be hit by e5 once the knights have traded on c6, so White decides how sharp the game gets.

Closes the d6 hole with a pawn and frees the dark-squared bishop, heading for a compact centre of pawns on d6 and e6. Black gives up some space but has few weaknesses and keeps the central breaks; White chooses between a quiet and a sharp plan.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Taimanov Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..background: Mark Taimanov's idea was to play 5...a6, which prevents Nb5. In recent years 5...Qc7 has been the more usual move order.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..strategy: Takes b5 away from White's knights, but spends a move without developing a piece. When White trades knights on c6, Black's recapture leaves a looser pawn structure against a White lead in development, which has made equality hard to reach.

A calm developing move: the bishop heads for quick castling without blocking the d-file, so the queen keeps guarding the d4 knight. White commits to nothing yet and relies on the solid centre, hoping for a small, lasting space advantage.

Develops the bishop to an active square where it supports the d4 knight and prepares queen to d2, long castling and a kingside pawn attack, though quiet short castling stays possible. White keeps the centre under control; the fight is for the d4 outpost.

Takes e5 away and builds a broad centre with a kingside attack in mind. It uses a tempo before the bishops are out and loosens the e3 square and the diagonal to g1, and Black answers with calm development and a trade of the strong knight.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Scheveningen Variation, Modern Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..strategy: Develops the last knight with a hit on e4 and completes the small centre of pawns on d6 and e6. Black can castle quickly in a solid position with both ...d5 and ...e5 in reserve as central breaks, while White has few targets.

Develops the bishop and prepares to castle, supporting the d6 pawn and keeping the compact centre. Black holds back the last knight and keeps the choice of set-up open, a sound if slightly passive plan that puts no immediate pressure on e4.

Takes b5 away from White's knights for good and prepares ...b5, a useful move in nearly every set-up Black reaches here. It spends a tempo on the queenside before castling, but White's centre offers no quick target, so Black can still develop in comfort.

The sharp main move: the knight eyes d6 and c7, and with the queen behind it Nd6+ is a real threat that would win the bishop pair. Black has to deal with it at once, and the incursion makes d6 the focus of the whole middlegame.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Four Knights Variation, Exchange Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..background: This option has become more popular over time, but it remains less popular than 6.Ndb5.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..strategy: Trades the d4 knight for the one on c6 to gain a tempo: if Black recaptures with the b-pawn, e5 hits the f6 knight and drives it back. White gets space and the initiative at the price of releasing the central tension; the e5 pawn needs care and the lines are double-edged.

Develops quietly and keeps the d-file open, so the queen still supports the d4 knight. White prepares to castle and aims for a small, lasting edge, but gives up the sharp pressure of Ndb5, and Black can reach a calm game or pin the c3 knight with ...Bb4.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Four Knights Variation, Sveshnikov Transfer
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..strategy: Plugs the d6 hole with a pawn and prepares ...e5, heading for a structure with a backward d6 pawn and a weak d5 square. Black accepts that lasting weakness in return for active pieces, central space and play against the knight on b5.

Pins the c3 knight against the king, so e4 is effectively undefended and ...Nxe4 is threatened. White has to react, and the bishop may take on c3, which gives up the bishop pair for easy development and central play.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Four Knights Variation, Cobra Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..strategy: Brings the bishop to an active diagonal where it covers d6 and eyes f2. But White can still invade on the dark squares around c7 and d6, and the main line runs through a series of exchanges that can end in a drawish endgame.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Taimanov Variation, Bastrikov Variation, English Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6 5..strategy: The most common move: the bishop develops actively and guards the d4 knight, so ...Nxd4 can be met by Bxd4. White keeps the choice between long castling with a kingside pawn storm and a quieter set-up, so Black needs a plan that works against both.

The most aggressive move: the knight attacks the queen and forces it to move at once, with a gain of time. It also eyes d6 and a7, but it leaves the centre and White's development lags, so Black has time to settle.

Develops the king's bishop without blocking the d-file, so the queen keeps guarding d4, and prepares to castle short. A quieter plan than the main move: White aims for a slow, solid game and Black gets time for the queenside.

Takes b5 away from White's knights for good, so the queen can no longer be harassed there, and prepares ...b5 and ...Bb7 for queenside play. Black has a compact, safe position, and the game becomes a manoeuvring fight for the d4 outpost and the queenside.

Develops the last knight with a hit on e4, which only the c3 knight guards. With the queen on c7 covering e5, White has no e5 push against the knight, so Black can castle quickly or pin the c3 knight. The modern, flexible way to finish development.

Trades off White's best-placed piece at once, which eases Black's cramp. But White recaptures with the queen, which comes to the centre, while Black has spent a tempo on a trade that develops nothing new. A sound but unambitious choice.

Takes b5 away from White's knights and starts the queenside expansion that Black needs, because the bishop on e3 prepares a kingside pawn storm with long castling. The usual result is a race of attacks on opposite wings.

Develops with a hit on e4, which only the c3 knight guards, and holds the a-pawn back for now. But the bishop on e3 supports an attacking set-up with queen to d2 and long castling, and Black must meet a kingside pawn storm without queenside counterplay under way.

Removes the strong knight at once and eases Black's cramp. White can retake with the queen, or with the bishop, which ...e5 then sends back. Either way Black has not developed another piece, and the e-pawn advance would weaken d5.

Steps out of the knight's attack to a square that still covers d6, so the knight's jump there has no sting. The queen is slightly offside and Black has lost a tempo, but the knight has left the centre and White's development lags too.

Retreats the queen out of the attack but does not defend d6, since the d7 pawn blocks the file: Nd6+ Bxd6 Qxd6 gives White the bishop pair and a queen on d6 while Black has lost two tempi. A passive reaction that hands White the initiative.
Hits the knight but forgets that the queen is attacked: Nxc7+ wins the queen outright.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Defends the attacked e4 pawn with a developing move and keeps the knight on d4 in place. White's development stays flexible and harmonious; the tempting 5.e5 would lose a pawn to ...Qa5+, which hits the king and then takes on e5.

Develops and defends e4, but the bishop blocks the queen's guard of the d4 knight, which Black can challenge at once with ...Nc6. Black reaches equality without difficulty, so White gets less than with Nc3.
Attacks the knight, but 5...Qa5+ comes with check and, once it is blocked, the queen takes the e5 pawn for nothing. A common reflex that simply loses a pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Scheveningen Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: The Scheveningen first came to international attention at the 1923 tournament in Scheveningen, where several players, among them Max Euwe against Géza Maróczy, played it. It became popular in the 1920s and has been advocated by many grandmasters, such as Garry Kasparov.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Builds a small centre of pawns on d6 and e6, which controls e5 and d5 and keeps the f6 knight pressing on e4. Black accepts less space for a sound structure with few weaknesses and several central breaks; White decides how sharp the game gets.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Gaw-Paw Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Attacks the d4 knight, but the queen defends it, so nothing is really threatened. Black spends a tempo on an early queen sortie while White keeps developing, and the queen on b6 can become a target.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Pin Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Considered theoretically suspect, but tactics can be hard to calculate for an unprepared White.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Pins the c3 knight so that e4 is effectively undefended, a threat that an unprepared White can find awkward. It is considered suspect because White simply strikes in the centre with e5, driving the f6 knight away from the e4 pressure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Pin Variation, Koch Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The principled reply: the f6 knight is attacked at once, and the pin on c3 leaves Black short of good squares for it. White gains space and sends the queen to g4 to hit g7, so Black has to defend precisely; in return the e5 pawn may become a target.

A quiet developing move that defends e4 for good and takes the sting out of the pin. But the bishop blocks the queen's guard of the d4 knight, which Black can attack at once with a pawn, so White gets less than with the active alternative.

A sharp sidestep from the main line: the knight eyes d6 and c7, and Nd6+ would trade it for Black's dark-squared bishop. Grabbing e4 is met by Qg4, which attacks both the knight and g7 and gives White strong compensation.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Pin Variation, Jaffe Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Attacks the d4 knight with a pawn, and nothing defends the knight because Bd3 blocks the queen, so it has to move. Black gains the centre and space; the price is a weakened d5 square and a backward d-pawn, while the pin on the c3 knight stays.

Challenges the d4 knight, which Bd3 has left without the queen's support. After the trade on c6 Black recaptures with the b-pawn, keeps the pin on the c3 knight and prepares ...d5 against e4; White's e5 hitting the f6 knight is the point to watch.

A solid reply that guards the e5 square against the pawn push and keeps the pin on the c3 knight. It leaves the d4 knight alone, so White can castle and develop freely, and Black's centre is safe but gives no chance to strike first.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Scheveningen Variation, Classical Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Also known as the Maroczy Variation, not to be confused with the Maroczy Bind. Anatoly Karpov used it to great effect, and it has many followers.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: The patient main line: the bishop prepares quick castling and keeps White's pawn structure flexible, so White can build a kingside attack or a central grip later. Black gets time to finish development and choose between queenside counterplay and a central break; the theory is deep.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Scheveningen Variation, Keres Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Paul Keres introduced 6.g4 in 1943. Players today often avoid it by playing 5...a6 first, an idea Garry Kasparov popularised.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Gains kingside space and threatens g5 to drive the f6 knight away. The e6 pawn has blocked the c8 bishop's route to g4, so the advance is hard to challenge. White commits to a sharp attack with the king still in the centre, and Black must react at once.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Scheveningen Variation, Matanovic Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Takes e5 from Black and builds a broad pawn centre, preparing quick development and a kingside attack. The move weakens the e1-h4 diagonal and the e3 square, so White has to be careful, but it makes Black's ...e5 break hard to carry out.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Sozin Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..background: Named after Bobby Fischer and the Russian master Veniamin Sozin, who originated it in the 1930s.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: Aims the bishop at e6, where the knight and bishop attack the pawn and the f7 pawn and c8 bishop defend it, so ideas of a sacrifice there hover over Black's development. The game is sharp, and Black must develop with the pressure on e6 in mind.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Scheveningen Variation, Fianchetto Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: A slow set-up: the bishop will guard e4 from g2, but it costs time that Black uses to finish development, and White has none of the attacking chances of the sharper moves. Neither side is under pressure, and Black has an easy game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..name: Sicilian Defence: Scheveningen Variation, Vitolins Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5..strategy: A check that achieves little: Black blocks with a developing move, and the bishop has no useful future on b5 and soon has to trade or retreat, losing time. White has given up the bishop's useful diagonal for nothing.

Completes the kingside development and prepares castling, so Black's king is safe before White's attack builds up. The bishop also supports the d6 pawn and the f6 knight, keeping the small centre compact for the later counterplay.

Brings the knight to the centre with pressure on d4, asking White to trade or hold the tension; a recapture by the queen costs White a tempo. Black stays compact with pawns on d6 and e6 and can castle quickly, keeping the game flexible.

Takes b5 away from White's pieces and prepares queenside expansion, a useful move in almost every set-up. Black keeps the choice of how to develop the other pieces open, at the price of one more pawn move before castling.

Develops with a hit on the d4 knight and an eye on e5, so White must decide at once whether to keep the knight or trade. Trading relieves Black's cramped position, and f4 has loosened White's own structure, so the fight stays sharp.
Develops the bishop and prepares castling, a sound, patient reply to the pawn move that has committed White's kingside. Black keeps the other pieces flexible and meets any attack from a safe king.

Stops Nb5 and prepares queenside play, a useful move in almost every set-up. White's f4 has committed the kingside pawns, so Black can afford to wait and develop after seeing where White's bishop goes.
